### FILE: stdlib/hash.caspien
```
// A simple, generic hash function -- works uniformly on *any* type T
// (primitive types; see the note on structs below) by hashing its own raw
// in-memory bytes, sidestepping the fact that this language has no
// generic bounds (`T: SomeInterface`) and primitives can't have methods
// at all (so a duck-typed "T must have a .hash() method" requirement,
// the more usual approach, isn't available here).
//
// The hash is real 64-bit FNV-1a (the published algorithm, not a
// look-alike): start from the offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325 and, for
// every byte in order, `h = bits_xor(h, byte)` and then
// `h = h * 0x100000001b3` (the 64-bit FNV prime), wrapping mod 2^64.
// It used to be a multiplicative `h*33 + byte` rolling hash because the
// language had no XOR; since `bits_xor` exists it is the real thing. The
// bytes of a value are fed in memory order (least significant byte
// first for an integer), so `hashOf:<u32>(7)` is FNV-1a-64 of the four
// bytes 07 00 00 00. Published vectors (checked by tests/fnv1a_test.caspien):
// "" -> 0xcbf29ce484222325, "a" -> 0xaf63dc4c8601ec8c,
// "foobar" -> 0x85944171f73967e8.
//
// `fnv1a64Bytes` is the same hash over an arbitrary byte buffer (a
// string's characters, a struct's bytes copied out through `memcopy`,
// ...); `hashOf` is just "copy the value's bytes into a scratch buffer,
// call `fnv1a64Bytes`".
//
// A struct T cannot be passed to `hashOf` (its parameter is a plain
// by-value `imut T`, and a by-value struct parameter is illegal in this
// language, so the instantiation is rejected for any struct T) -- hash a
// struct by copying its bytes into a buffer yourself and calling
// `fnv1a64Bytes`. Beware that a struct's padding bytes are not
// initialised, so only a padding-free struct has a stable hash.
import "libc.caspien"

/** FNV-1a, 64 bit, over `byteCount` bytes starting at `p`. `byteCount` 0 gives the offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325. */
@pub
func fnv1a64Bytes(p: raw imut u8, byteCount: mut u64) mut u64{
	let h = mut 0xcbf29ce484222325
	unsafe{
		for i in 0..byteCount{
			let byteVal = mut deref(p + i) as u64
			h = bits_xor(h, byteVal)
			h = h * 0x100000001b3
		}
	}
	return h
}

@pub
func hashOf<T>(x: imut T) mut u64{
	let byteCount = mut sizeof(T)
	let:<raw mut u8> buf = null
	let h = mut 0
	unsafe{
		buf = mut malloc(byteCount)
		memcopy(buf, byteCount, raw x)
		h = fnv1a64Bytes(buf, byteCount)
		free(buf)
	}
	return h
}
```

```
// A general-purpose HashMap<T,T> -- key and value share one type
// parameter. Real `impl<T> HashMap<T>` methods, `_self` a genuine
// `ref` -- **not** a plain (no-storage) value, corrected for the same
// reason `DynamicArray<T>` was (see its own file-level comment for
// the full reasoning): a plain `_self` never actually made mutations
// visible to the caller (that was an overclaim), and separately gave
// every method here a silent null-dereference hole, since `owns`
// values genuinely can be `null` in this type system and
// `checkDot`'s liveness-proof restriction only ever fires on a value
// with real storage. No `unsafe` anywhere in this file at all -- each
// method's own probing walk used a bare `loop{...}` until `for` could
// express it. Key equality uses "==" directly on T -- confirmed to
// type-check for two struct values of the same type, not just
// primitives ("checkComparison" only requires both sides share a
// base type, no restriction to numeric/pointer types at all).
//
// REWRITTEN under the same precondition philosophy
// `dynamic_array.caspien`/`string.caspien` were ("want me to write on
// something or retrieve out of it? No, I pass the null check
// responsibility to you," confirmed directly): `set`/`get`/`contains`
// all now take `_self` as `ref some (imut|mut) self`, never a plain
// `ref` -- the caller must already have proven non-null via
// `match Some(_self){...}` before the call is even legal, so none of
// these three needs its own internal `match Some(_self){...}`/
// fallback for that case any more. **`cap != 0` is a genuinely
// different kind of precondition, kept as an internal check, not
// pushed onto the caller** -- unlike a null `_self` (which `some`
// already has a caller-side proof mechanism for) or an out-of-bounds
// index (which `@lock`/`match ... in/into ...` already has one for),
// there is no existing precondition-proof shape in this language that
// could express "this map's own capacity field is nonzero" as a
// caller-side obligation at all -- `_self.capacity` is an ordinary
// runtime field read, not a parameter or a literal a `match` could
// name. A zero-capacity map is a real, if degenerate, construction
// (`new HashMap:<T>(k, v, mut 0)` type-checks and compiles
// cleanly), so this stays a genuine, internal runtime guard -- `set`
// silently no-ops on one, `get`/`contains` still return their own
// caller-supplied `defaultValue`/`false`, the same fallback pattern
// `DynamicArray<T>::get` already established for its own "there's no
// safe generic value to fabricate for an arbitrary T" case.
//
// The slot for a key starts at `hashOf(key) % capacity` and is probed linearly. `hashOf` is real 64-bit FNV-1a over the key's bytes (see
// `hash.caspien`; it used to be a multiplicative `h*33 + byte` hash), so the order in which keys land in slots differs from the old
// hash's, but the map's observable behaviour (set/get/contains/count) does not depend on it. A key type must be a non-struct type (the
// `hashOf` parameter is a by-value `imut T`).
//
// `HashMap` is built with its constructor, `new HashMap:<u64>(k, v, cap)`.
import "hash.caspien"

@pub
struct HashMapEntry<T>{@pub{
	key: mut T
	value: mut T
	occupied: mut bool
}}

@pub
struct HashMap<T>{@pub{
	slots: owns some mut dynarray(imut HashMapEntry<T>)
	capacity: mut u64
	count: mut u64
}}

/** `new HashMap:<T>(defaultKey, defaultValue, capacity)` -- `defaultKey`/`defaultValue` seed every initially-empty slot (never read as real data -- `occupied` starts `false` everywhere); there's no default-construction mechanism for an arbitrary T to fall back on instead. `capacity` is fixed for this map's entire lifetime -- see the file-level note on rehashing. `@throws`: the `dyn` and `resize` (out of memory) can fail; the caught error is simply re-thrown to the caller. */
@pub
@throws
impl<T> constructor for HashMap<T>(defaultKey: mut T, defaultValue: mut T, capacity: mut u64) self{
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	let seed = mut HashMapEntry:<T>{key= defaultKey, value= defaultValue, occupied= mut false}
	let slots = mut ? dyn:<HashMapEntry:<T>>([])
	let grownSlots = mut ? resize(slots, capacity, seed)
	return HashMap:<T>{slots= grownSlots, capacity= capacity, count= mut 0}
}

@pub
impl<T> HashMap<T>{
	/** Inserts, or updates the value if `key` is already present. `void`, so `match Some(_self){...}` with no `else` needs nothing further -- a null `_self` simply makes this a no-op. `cap` is captured once and proven nonzero (`u64` is unsigned, so `!=0` alone is sufficient -- see CLAUDE.md, "match") before either `%` below -- a map's own capacity is a caller-supplied `u64`, never provably nonzero at the type level, so this needs a genuine runtime proof, not just a literal-divisor exemption; a zero-capacity map (a genuinely degenerate construction) simply no-ops instead of dividing by it. */
	@pub
	func set(_self: ref some mut self, key: mut T, value: mut T) void{
		let cap = mut _self.capacity
		match cap != 0{
			let h = mut hashOf:<T>(imut key)
			let startIdx = mut (h % cap)
			for steps in 0..cap{
				let idx = mut ((startIdx + steps) % cap)
				match idx into _self.slots{
					let entry = mut _self.slots[idx]
					if !entry.occupied{
						_self.slots[idx] = mut HashMapEntry:<T>{key= key, value= value, occupied= mut true}
						_self.count = mut (_self.count + 1)
						break
					}
					if entry.key == key{
						_self.slots[idx] = mut HashMapEntry:<T>{key= key, value= value, occupied= mut true}
						break
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}

	/** `defaultValue` is returned when `key` isn't present, or when `_self.capacity` is zero (a degenerate construction, see this file's own header comment) -- there's no way to signal "not found" separately without a real option/result type, which this language doesn't have yet; use `contains` first if the distinction matters. */
	@pub
	func get(_self: ref some imut self, key: mut T, defaultValue: mut T) mut T{
		let cap = mut _self.capacity
		match cap != 0{
			let h = mut hashOf:<T>(imut key)
			let startIdx = mut (h % cap)
			for steps in 0..cap{
				let idx = mut ((startIdx + steps) % cap)
				match idx in _self.slots{
					let entry = mut _self.slots[idx]
					if !entry.occupied{
						return defaultValue
					}
					if entry.key == key{
						return entry.value
					}
				}
			}
			return defaultValue
		}
		return defaultValue
	}

	@pub
	func contains(_self: ref some imut self, key: mut T) mut bool{
		let cap = mut _self.capacity
		match cap != 0{
			let h = mut hashOf:<T>(imut key)
			let startIdx = mut (h % cap)
			for steps in 0..cap{
				let idx = mut ((startIdx + steps) % cap)
				match idx in _self.slots{
					let entry = mut _self.slots[idx]
					if !entry.occupied{
						return mut false
					}
					if entry.key == key{
						return mut true
					}
				}
			}
			return mut false
		}
		return mut false
	}
}
```

```
// A handful of C standard library functions, made available via
// 'extern' for linking against libc in the final assembly. Calling any
// of these requires 'unsafe' code (see CLAUDE.md, "extern and export")
// -- declaring/importing them does not.
//
// Signature notes:
//   - printf's format string and every fixed/variadic argument are
//     never validated against each other by this compiler (no printf-
//     format-string checking exists) -- getting the format string
//     wrong is exactly as unsafe here as it is in C itself.
//   - putchar/getchar move a character as a full word (mirroring C's
//     own "int", not a narrower char type) -- putchar returns the
//     character written back (or an EOF-ish sentinel on failure),
//     getchar returns the character read (or EOF).
//   - strlen takes a Caspien 'string' directly, since a Caspien string
//     is already the pointer C's 'const char*' expects.
//   - malloc/realloc/free operate on raw bytes ('raw u8') -- the
//     single shared source for these three, imported by anything that
//     needs real heap allocation (the ghost table, the generic 'hashOf'
//     byte-hasher, the SHA-256 streaming context) rather than each declaring its own independent
//     copy, which would conflict the instant two such files were
//     imported into the same program together (a real mistake caught
//     exactly that way while building 'hashOf').
//   - abort() genuinely never returns (it terminates the process) --
//     this compiler's own "every path must return" check has no way
//     to know that about an arbitrary extern, though, so a call to it
//     still needs to be followed by *something* satisfying that check
//     structurally. Real code (e.g. DynamicArray<T>::get) follows it
//     with a break-free "loop{}" for exactly this reason -- genuinely
//     dead code in any real run (abort() has already ended the
//     process before it could ever be reached), there purely to
//     satisfy the type checker, the same well-established pattern
//     other languages use their own "unreachable()"-style markers for.
//     Used specifically in place of silently looping forever on a
//     genuine invariant violation (the actual bug this replaced) --
//     crashing loudly and immediately beats hanging silently forever.
//   - clock() returns CPU time consumed by the process (clock_t,
//     scaled by CLOCKS_PER_SEC), not true monotonic wall-clock elapsed
//     time -- "just extern clock() for me... we'll move forward with
//     that limitation for now," confirmed directly: a genuine,
//     accepted limitation (it won't count time spent blocked on I/O or
//     asleep), chosen specifically because, unlike a true monotonic
//     clock (POSIX's own clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, ...), not
//     ANSI C, and takes an out-parameter pointer rather than returning
//     a scalar), clock() is genuinely as universal and simply-shaped
//     as strlen/printf themselves -- a plain, argument-less call
//     returning one scalar. No CLOCKS_PER_SEC constant exposed here --
//     not asked for.
//   - popen()/pclose()/fgets()/fputs() -- "spawn"/"StdOut"/"StdIn,"
//     confirmed directly, are built on top of these, in
//     "stdlib/process.caspien," never called directly by ordinary
//     code. "Ok if you could just give me one directional handles for
//     now that would be good," confirmed directly -- popen()'s own
//     mode string ("r" xor "w", never both at once) is exactly why a
//     spawned process here only ever supports reading *or* writing,
//     never both on the same handle (a genuine, real limitation, the
//     same "accepted for now" shape clock()'s own CPU-time-not-wall-
//     clock limitation already has -- true bidirectional access needs
//     several lower-level calls orchestrated together per platform
//     (pipe()/fork()/dup2()/exec() on POSIX; CreateProcess() with pipe
//     handles on Windows), not one clean extern binding the way this
//     is). fgets()'s own declared return type here (`static imut
//     string`) doesn't literally match its real C signature (`char*`,
//     not `const char*`) -- the same "best-fit Caspien approximation,
//     not a literal signature match" already true of malloc/realloc's
//     own declared return type here (`raw mut u8`, not C's `void*`).
extern printf(static imut string,...) void
extern putchar(mut u64) mut u64
extern getchar() mut u64
extern strlen(static imut string) mut u64
extern malloc(mut u64) raw mut u8
extern realloc(raw mut u8, mut u64) raw mut u8
extern free(raw imut u8) void
extern abort() void
extern clock() mut u64
// "c_sleep," not "sleep" -- "sleep" itself is now a reserved language
// keyword (see "sleep(...)" in caspien-compiler's own CLAUDE.md), so
// the real C library function can no longer be *declared* under its own
// literal name (an extern's name and a keyword can't share a spelling
// any more than an extern and an ordinary function can) -- but the real
// C library still only ever exports it *linked* under that exact
// literal "sleep" symbol, so "@link_name(sleep)" is required here:
// without it, this would link against a nonexistent "c_sleep" symbol

extern c_sleep(mut u64) mut u64
extern popen(static imut string, static imut string) raw mut u8
extern pclose(raw mut u8) mut u64
extern fgets(raw mut u8, mut u64, raw mut u8) static imut string
extern fputs(static imut string, raw mut u8) mut u64

//     bytecode has no real function-pointer *value* type distinct from
```

```
// "So make_safe_args is user written, but the expected normal
// behaviour is the one in the stdlib," confirmed directly -- this
// file. "make_safe_args returns owned memory, but make_safe_args
// doesnt take ownership of the actual real arguments passed to main -
// it copies them," confirmed directly: every byte of every argv
// string is read via `memcopy` into freshly-allocated dynarrays of
// this program's own; nothing here ever frees, or keeps a live
// pointer into, the C runtime's own argv/argc memory at all.
//
// Every pointer walked here is kept as 'raw mut u8' throughout, never
// 'raw mut char' or 'raw mut raw mut char' directly -- confirmed
// directly that '++' (this language's only pointer-arithmetic
// operator; there is no '+'/'+=' on a raw pointer at all) only accepts
// a numeric base type, rejecting 'char' and rejecting a pointer-to-
// pointer identically. Reinterpreted via `memcopy` (the same "read/
// write raw bytes through a pointer" mechanism this whole file already
// leans on) wherever the real, typed value underneath is actually
// needed.
import "libc.caspien"

@pub
@make_safe_args
@throws
func make_safe_args(argc: imut s32, argv: raw mut raw mut char) owns some mut dynarray(imut dynarray(imut char)){
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	// "int being the appropriate equivalent to C's int type,"
	// confirmed directly, resolved to 's32' -- but every dynarray
	// operation here needs a plain 'u64' count, and 'as' only ever
	// widens within one signedness family (s32 can't become u64
	// that way at all). argc is always non-negative in practice,
	// so a zero-extending 4-byte 'memcopy' into an already-zeroed
	// u64 local is exactly right -- the same "read raw bytes
	// through a pointer" mechanism 'hash.caspien' already uses for
	// an unrelated reason.
	let count = mut 0
	unsafe{
		memcopy(raw count, mut 4, raw argc)
	}

	// UPDATE (throwing 'dyn'/'resize'): "new throws, but dyn and
	// resize dont, they need to use the same pattern as new,"
	// confirmed directly -- every one of these can fail (out of
	// memory) too, now requiring the identical 'try'/'catch'
	// wrapping 'new' already needed; each is wrapped individually
	// and its caught error simply re-thrown, same as everywhere else
	// in this file. The nested inner "dyn([mut 'x'])" inside
	// "outer"'s own array literal needs no separate wrap of its own
	// -- the one 'try'/'catch' around the whole "dyn([dyn([...])])"
	// expression already covers it, at any depth (see
	// TypeChecker.insideThrowingAllocContext's own doc comment).
	let outer = mut ? dyn([dyn([mut 'x'])])
	let fillValue = mut ? dyn([mut 'x'])
	outer = ? resize(outer, count, fillValue)

	// argv itself, reinterpreted once as a byte pointer to walk
	// 8 bytes (one pointer width) per argument.
	let:<raw mut u8> cur = null
	unsafe{
		memcopy(raw cur, mut 8, raw argv)
	}
	let oi = mut 0
	for i in 0..count{
		let:<raw mut u8> strPtr = null
		unsafe{
			memcopy(raw strPtr, mut 8, cur)
		}

		// Determine this argument's own length by scanning for a
		// NUL byte.
		let len = mut 0
		let scan = mut strPtr
		unsafe{
			loop{
				let b = mut 0
				memcopy(raw b, mut 1, scan)
				if b == mut 0{
					break
				}
				len = mut (len + 1)
				scan++
			}
		}

		// Copy this argument's own `len` bytes, one at a time, into
		// a freshly-sized dynarray(char) -- this program's own,
		// independent copy.
		let inner = mut ? dyn([mut 'x'])
		inner = ? resize(inner, len, mut 'x')
		let copyFrom = mut strPtr
		let ii = mut 0
		match ii into inner{
			unsafe{
				loop{
					if ii >= len{
						break
					}
					let b2 = mut 0
					memcopy(raw b2, mut 1, copyFrom)
					let ch = mut 'x'
					memcopy(raw ch, mut 1, raw b2)
					inner[ii] = mut ch
					copyFrom++
					ii = mut (ii + 1)
				}
			}
		}

		match oi into outer{
			outer[oi] = mut inner
		}
		oi = mut (oi + 1)
		// Advance `cur` by one full pointer width (8 bytes). `cur` is a
		// `raw u8`, so `+=` moves it by that many bytes.
		cur += 8
	}

	return outer
}
```

```
// The real "@par_call" -- called by the compiler's own "par foo(...)"
// desugaring (see caspien-compiler's own CLAUDE.md, "par"/"await"
// real-thread desugaring) with the trampoline's own address (`fn`) and
// the freshly-constructed, already-`gt_register`ed handle pointer
// (`handle`, erased to a bare "raw mut u8" -- the fixed shape every
// "@par_call"/"@await_call" must have, since the concrete
// "AsyncHandle_<T>"/hidden-handle struct varies per "@async" function
// and this must be one single, fixed-signature function for the whole
// compilation unit).
//
```

```
func sha256Digest(state: raw imut u32, digest: raw mut u8) void{

// Streaming context: a heap state (8 words), a 64-byte pending buffer, the pending byte count and the total byte count.
@pub
struct Sha256Ctx{@pub{
	state: raw mut u32
	pending: raw mut u8
	pendingCount: mut u64
	totalCount: mut u64
}}

/** Starts a hash: allocates the state and the pending buffer inside `ctx`. Release with `sha256Release`. */
@pub
func sha256Begin(ctx: auto mut Sha256Ctx) void{
	unsafe{
		ctx.state = mut sha256NewState()
		ctx.pending = mut malloc(64)
		ctx.pendingCount = mut 0
		ctx.totalCount = mut 0
	}
}

/** Feeds `byteCount` bytes at `data` into the hash. Any number of calls, any split of the message. Bytes are collected in the 64-byte pending buffer and compressed from there (one compression call site). */
@pub
func sha256Update(ctx: auto mut Sha256Ctx, data: raw imut u8, byteCount: mut u64) void{
	unsafe{
		let done = mut 0
		ctx.totalCount = mut (ctx.totalCount + byteCount)
		loop{
			if ctx.pendingCount == 64{
				sha256Compress(ctx.state, ctx.pending)
				ctx.pendingCount = mut 0
			}else{
				let remaining = mut (byteCount - done)
				if remaining == 0{
					break
				}
				let take = mut (64 - ctx.pendingCount)
				if take > remaining{
					take = remaining
				}
				memcopy(ctx.pending + ctx.pendingCount, take, data + done)
				ctx.pendingCount = mut (ctx.pendingCount + take)
				done = done + take
			}
		}
	}
}

/** Pads, finishes and writes the 32-byte digest to `digest`. The context must not be updated afterwards (call `sha256Begin` again to reuse it). */
@pub
func sha256Finish(ctx: auto mut Sha256Ctx, digest: raw mut u8) void{
	unsafe{
		let bitCount = mut (ctx.totalCount * 8)
		let pad = mut 0x80
		let zero = mut 0
		memcopy(ctx.pending + ctx.pendingCount, mut 1, raw pad)
		let from = mut (ctx.pendingCount + 1)
		let lastBlock = mut (from <= 56)
		loop{
			if lastBlock{
				for i in from..56{
					memcopy(ctx.pending + i, mut 1, raw zero)
				}
				for k in 0..8{
					let sh = mut wrap:<u64>(56 - 8 * k)
					let byteVal = mut wrap:<u8>(bits_right(bitCount, sh))
					memcopy(ctx.pending + (56 + k), mut 1, raw byteVal)
				}
			}else{
				for i in from..64{
					memcopy(ctx.pending + i, mut 1, raw zero)
				}
			}
			sha256Compress(ctx.state, ctx.pending)
			if lastBlock{
				break
			}
			lastBlock = true
			from = mut 0
		}
		sha256Digest(ctx.state, digest)
		ctx.pendingCount = mut 0
	}
}

/** Frees what `sha256Begin` allocated. */
@pub
func sha256Release(ctx: auto mut Sha256Ctx) void{
	unsafe{
		sha256FreeState(ctx.state)
		free(ctx.pending)
	}
}

/** One-shot SHA-256: hashes the `byteCount` bytes at `data` and writes the 32-byte digest to `digest`. `byteCount` may be 0 (`data` may then be null). */
@pub
func sha256(data: raw imut u8, byteCount: mut u64, digest: raw mut u8) void{
	unsafe{
		let ctx = mut Sha256Ctx{state= null, pending= null, pendingCount= mut 0, totalCount= mut 0}
		sha256Begin(auto ctx)
		sha256Update(auto ctx, data, byteCount)
		sha256Finish(auto ctx, digest)
		sha256Release(auto ctx)
	}
}
```

```
// The real "@sleep" -- called by the compiler's own "sleep(...)"
// keyword (see TypeChecker.checkSleepCall, and caspien-compiler's own
// CLAUDE.md, "'sleep' introduced as a keyword") whenever it's used
// anywhere in the compilation unit; using "sleep(...)" without a
// function decorated "@sleep" imported somewhere is a compile-time
// error ("requires a function decorated '@sleep' to exist..."), the
// same shape "@par_call"/"@await_call" already have for "par"/"await".
//
// A pure wrapper around the real C library "sleep" -- "have it take
// the same arguments as the function in C," confirmed directly: the
// real POSIX signature is "unsigned int sleep(unsigned int seconds)",
// approximated here (the same widening this stdlib's other C wrappers
// already use, e.g. putchar/getchar's own "int" -> "u64") as a single
// plain "u64" parameter (the number of seconds to sleep) returning a
// plain "u64" (the number of seconds left unslept, if a signal
// interrupted it early -- 0 on ordinary completion). "@sleep" itself
// enforces this exact shape at compile time (TypeChecker.
// requireSleepSignature) -- a function decorated "@sleep" with any
// other signature is rejected before it can ever reach here.
//
// The real extern this wraps is declared as "c_sleep," not "sleep" --
// see libc.caspien's own comment on why "sleep" itself was no longer
// available to name it.
import "libc.caspien"

@sleep
@pub
func sleep_call(seconds: mut u64) mut u64{
	let remaining = mut 0
	unsafe{
		remaining = mut c_sleep(seconds)
	}
	return remaining
}
```

```
// A new, owned, growable/mutable String type -- distinct from the
// built-in `string` primitive, which is fixed, read-only, and used
// for literals and C interop.
//
// REWRITTEN under the same precondition philosophy
// `dynamic_array.caspien` was ("want me to write on something or
// retrieve out of it? No, I pass the null check responsibility to
// you," confirmed directly): every method takes `_self`/`other` as
// `ref some (imut|mut) self`, never a plain `ref` -- the caller must
// already have proven non-null via `match Some(...)` before the call
// is even legal, so no method here needs its own internal
// `match Some(_self){...}`/fallback at all. `length` is gone as a
// field entirely -- "length isnt needed in String or DynamicArray,
// its built into a dyn," confirmed directly; every read of the
// character count now reads `len(_self.chars.backing)` directly.
//
// **Zero `unsafe`/`raw` anywhere in this file's own public API, or
// internally, at all.** `String`'s from-text construction used to walk a `malloc`'d
// buffer one byte at a time via `strlen`/`memcopy`; `concat` (its `string` overload)
// had an identical internal walk. Both are now built directly on the
// extended `dyn(...)` builtin, which accepts a `static imut string`
// argument and returns a real, runtime-populated `dynarray(char)` with
// no memory access exposed to Caspien code at all (see CLAUDE.md's own
// "Dynarrays" section, and `dynamic_array_from_string_test.caspien`).
// `new String(text)` in particular is built from
// `new DynamicArray:<char>(dyn(text))`.
//
// `String` is built with its constructors, `new String()` (empty) and
// `new String(text)` (from a string literal), not with static methods:
// once a struct declares a constructor, its struct-literal form
// `String{...}` is legal only inside those constructors.
import "dynamic_array.caspien"
import "libc.caspien"

@pub
struct String{@pub{
	chars: owns some mut DynamicArray<char>
}}

/** `new String()` -- a genuinely empty String, zero characters. `@throws`: the nested `new DynamicArray:<char>()` (and its `dyn`) can fail (out of memory); the caught error is simply re-thrown to the caller. */
@pub
@throws
impl constructor for String() self{
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	let chars = mut ? new DynamicArray:<char>()
	return String{chars= chars}
}

/** `new String(text)` -- a String holding a copy of the string literal `text`. "Have dyn also take a static imut string, returning a dyn of chars," confirmed directly: `String` is a thin wrapper over a safe dynarray of chars, so nothing here needs `unsafe`. `@throws`: the `dyn` and the nested `new DynamicArray` can fail (out of memory); the caught error is simply re-thrown to the caller. */
@pub
@throws
impl constructor for String(text: static imut string) self{
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	let arr = mut ? dyn(text)
	let chars = mut ? new DynamicArray:<char>(arr)
	return String{chars= chars}
}

@pub
impl String{
	/**
	 * `myString.concat(myString, other)` -- appends another String's own
	 * characters (`other` may be `myString` itself, which doubles it -- this
	 * replaces the old `concatRef`, whose signature differed from this one only
	 * in mutability and so could not be an overload). Indexes `other.chars.backing` directly (never through
	 * `charAt`) so the per-character bounds proof is a genuine
	 * `match i in other.chars.backing{...}`, not a second, redundant
	 * internal check.
	 *
	 * `chars` is declared `owns some`, so `ref some` on `_self`/`other`
	 * is enough to reach `_self.chars.backing` directly: the type itself
	 * says `chars` is always present (every constructor sets it), and no
	 * method here needs a `match Some(...)` of its own.
	 */
	/** Now `@throws`: `appendChar` is itself `@throws` now (its own `pushBack` can fail -- see `appendChar`'s own doc comment), so this method must wrap every call to it and propagate the caught error to its own caller in turn. */
	@pub
	@throws
	func concat(_self: ref some mut self, other: ref some imut self) void{
		?catch(e){ throw e }
		let n = mut len(other.chars.backing)
		for i in 0..n{
			match i in other.chars.backing{
				? _self.appendChar(_self, other.chars.backing[i])
			}
		}
	}

	/** `myString.concat(myString, "literal text")` -- the overload of `concat` taking a plain Caspien string value instead of another `String` (chosen by argument type at the call site; formerly a separate method named `concatLiteral`). Appends via `dyn(other)` (a fresh, throwaway dynarray(char) populated from `other`'s own characters) rather than any raw memory walk. */
	/** Now `@throws`: its own `dyn(other)` and `appendChar` are both `@throws`-capable now (see their own doc comments), each wrapped here and its caught error propagated to this method's own caller in turn. */
	@pub
	@throws
	func concat(_self: ref some mut self, other: static imut string) void{
		?catch(e){ throw e }
		let otherChars = mut ? dyn(other)
		let n = mut len(otherChars)
		for i in 0..n{
			match i in otherChars{
				? _self.appendChar(_self, otherChars[i])
			}
		}
	}

	/** Now `@throws`: `DynamicArray::pushBack` is itself `@throws` now (its own `resize` can fail -- "new throws, but dyn and resize dont, they need to use the same pattern as new," confirmed directly), so this method must wrap that call and propagate the caught error to its own caller in turn -- the same cascade `sub` below already documents for `new String()`. */
	@pub
	@throws
	func appendChar(_self: ref some mut self, c: mut char) void{
		?catch(e){ throw e }
		? _self.chars.pushBack(_self.chars, c)
	}

	/** The substring from `start` (inclusive) to `end` (exclusive) -- two separate arguments, not one "0..12" range value: a bare `range` used as an ordinary (non-storage) parameter type is an "incomplete type" in this language. Now `@throws`: its own internal call to `new String()` is itself `@throws` now (see the `String()` constructor's own doc comment), so this method must wrap that call and propagate the caught error to its own caller in turn. */
	@pub
	@throws
	func sub(_self: ref some imut self, start: mut u64, end: mut u64) owns some mut String{
		?catch(e){ throw e }
		let result = mut ? new String()
		for i in start..end{
			match i in _self.chars.backing{
				? result.appendChar(result, _self.chars.backing[i])
			}
		}
		return result
	}

	/** Returns the index of the first occurrence of `target`, or `-1` when `target` isn't present -- there's no option/result type yet to signal that separately, so a negative `s64` is the sentinel (an index itself is never negative). Unlike the earlier version of this method, there is no internal null check on `_self` at all -- `ref some` already requires the caller to have proven that before the call was even legal. */
	@pub
	func firstIndexOf(_self: ref some imut self, target: mut char) mut s64{
		let n = mut len(_self.chars.backing)
		let position = mut -1
		for i in 0..n{
			position++
			match i in _self.chars.backing{
				if _self.chars.backing[i] == target{
					return position
				}
			}
		}
		return -1
	}

	/**
	 * Bounds-safe: out-of-range returns '\0'. `_self` needs no internal
	 * null check any more (`ref some`, proven by the caller), but this
	 * method still needs an ordinary
	 * `match i in _self.chars.backing{...}` for the index itself, rather
	 * than through a `@lock(match i in self.chars.backing)` precondition
	 * the way `DynamicArray<T>::get` now does. This is a real, narrower
	 * scope limitation, not an oversight: `@lock(match ...)`'s own
	 * grammar (`Parser.parseLockInQualifier`) only ever accepts a
	 * single-level `self.field`, never a nested chain like
	 * `self.chars.backing` -- there is currently no way to make
	 * bounds-proof through a nested struct member a caller-side
	 * precondition at all. Once that grammar is extended, this can
	 * become `@lock`-qualified exactly like `get`.
	 */
	@pub
	func charAt(_self: ref some imut self, i: mut u64) mut char{
		match i in _self.chars.backing{
			return _self.chars.backing[i]
		}
		return mut '\0'
	}

	/**
	 * Overwrites the character at index `i` with `c`, by composition: it
	 * hands the write straight to `DynamicArray::set` on the underlying
	 * `chars` (the same way `appendChar` hands off to `pushBack`), rather
	 * than writing into `backing` itself. `DynamicArray::set` is
	 * `@lock(match i into self.backing)` -- the caller must hold a write
	 * authorization for `i` -- so this method takes that proof itself with
	 * `match i into _self.chars.backing{...}` and out-of-range `i` is
	 * simply a no-op (mirroring `charAt`, which returns '\0' out of range).
	 */
	@pub
	func setCharAt(_self: ref some mut self, i: mut u64, c: mut char) void{
		match i into _self.chars.backing{
			_self.chars.set(_self.chars, i, c)
		}
	}
}
```

### FILE: tests/allocreorder_hob_check.sh
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Bytecode-level check for the Optimizer's VariableAllocationReorderingPass (`variable-allocation-reordering: on`): the order of each function's
# hoisted ALLOC run after the pass. It writes small hand-made HOB files to a temp dir, runs the prebuilt Optimizer on each with only that switch set
# and compares the ALLOC names, function by function, with what the pass is specified to produce. Run from anywhere:
#   tests/allocreorder_hob_check.sh        (needs Optimizer/out, i.e. the shipped prebuilt classes)
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
W=$(mktemp -d); cd "$W" || exit 1
export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=
bad=0
# fn <name> <alloc list "name:type ..."> [extra body lines]: a function whose ALLOC run is the given one; every variable is mentioned once by a PUSH
fn(){ printf 'FUNC_START %s\nRETURNS imut_void\n' "$1"; for a in $2; do printf 'ALLOC %s %s\n' "${a%%:*}" "${a#*:}"; done
  for a in $2; do case "${a%%:*}" in gt_*) ;; *) printf 'PUSH %s %s\nPOP ARG0 %s\n' "${a%%:*}" "${a#*:}" "${a#*:}";; esac; done
  printf "$3"; printf 'RET imut_void\nFUNC_END\n'; }
run(){ # <case> <switch value> ; reads <case>.hob
  printf 'variable-allocation-reordering: %s\n' "$2" > compiler.config
  java -cp "$ROOT/Optimizer/out" caspien.optimizer.Main -i "$1.hob" "$1.out" >/dev/null 2>&1
  awk '/^FUNC_START/{f=$2} /^ALLOC /{a[f]=a[f] " " $2} END{for(k in a) print k ":" a[k]}' "$1.out" | sort | tr '\n' ';' | sed 's/;$//'; }
check(){ got=$(run "$1" "${3:-on}"); if [ "$got" = "$2" ]; then echo "PASS $1"; else echo "FAIL $1: got [$got]"; echo "          want [$2]"; bad=1; fi; }
{ fn main 'a:mut_u8 b:mut_u64 c:mut_u8 d:mut_u64'; } > r1.hob
check r1 "main: b d a c"
{ fn main 'gt_routine_address:code_addr gt_error_message:static_imut_string a:mut_u8 b:mut_u64 c:mut_u16 d:mut_u32'; } > r2.hob
check r2 "main: gt_routine_address gt_error_message b d c a"
# x, y, z all 8 bytes: z is used inside a loop (weight 8), x and y once each: z first, then x, y in their original order
{ printf 'FUNC_START main\nRETURNS imut_void\nALLOC x mut_u64\nALLOC y mut_u64\nALLOC z mut_u64\nPUSH x mut_u64\nPUSH y mut_u64\n@L:\nPUSH z mut_u64\nJMP @L\nRET imut_void\nFUNC_END\n'; } > r3.hob
check r3 "main: z x y"
# a struct is as aligned as its widest member (the classId alone makes it 8)
{ printf 'STRUCT_START S\nSTRUCT_MEMBER ___type imut_u64\nSTRUCT_MEMBER a mut_u8\nSTRUCT_PADDING 7\nSTRUCT_END\nSTRUCT_START T\nSTRUCT_MEMBER a mut_u8\nSTRUCT_MEMBER b mut_u8\nSTRUCT_END\n'; fn main 'i:mut_u8 t:mut_T q:mut_u32 s:mut_S'; } > r4.hob
check r4 "main: s q i t"
{ printf 'FUNC_START main\nRETURNS imut_void\nALLOC a mut_u8\nALLOC b mut_u64\nASM_START\nASM_END\nRET imut_void\nFUNC_END\n'; } > r5.hob
check r5 "main: a b"
{ fn main 'a:mut_u8 b:mut_u64 c:mut_u8 d:mut_u64'; } > r6.hob
check r6 "main: a b c d" off
# only the leading contiguous ALLOC run is reordered: the ALLOC after a body line keeps its place
{ printf 'FUNC_START main\nRETURNS imut_void\nALLOC a mut_u8\nALLOC b mut_u64\nPUSH a mut_u8\nALLOC c mut_u64\nALLOC d mut_u8\nRET imut_void\nFUNC_END\n'; } > r7.hob
check r7 "main: b a c d"
# an unknown type (an enum) is 8-aligned, like the lowering treats it; pointers 8, arrays their element's, a range 8
{ fn main 'a:mut_u8 e:mut_Color p:raw_mut_u8 w:mut_u16[3] v:mut_u32[3] r:imut_range(0,mut_n)'; } > r8.hob
check r8 "main: e p r v w a"
# gt_error_message anywhere but right behind gt_routine_address: the function is left alone
{ fn main 'gt_routine_address:code_addr a:mut_u8 gt_error_message:static_imut_string b:mut_u64'; } > r9.hob
check r9 "main: gt_routine_address a gt_error_message b"
# a single slot / already-sorted runs / parameters: nothing to do
{ fn main 'a:mut_u64'; fn f 'b:mut_u64 c:mut_u8'; printf 'FUNC_START g\nRETURNS imut_void\nARG p mut_u8\nALLOC x mut_u8\nALLOC y mut_u64\nRET imut_void\nFUNC_END\n'; } > r10.hob
check r10 "f: b c;g: y x;main: a"
cd /; rm -rf "$W"; exit $bad
```

### FILE: tests/allocreorder_test.caspien
```
// Regression test for `variable-allocation-reordering`: a function whose locals are declared in the worst order for padding (u8, u64, u8, u64, ...)
// must compute the same results with the slots reordered: mixed widths written and read back in a loop, an array and a struct among them, parameters
// (which stay ahead of the locals), a function with owns/throw (whose gt_routine_address / gt_error_message slots stay first) and a catch that reads
// its own locals. Run with the switch off and on: the output must be identical, and the frame of `mixed` smaller with it on.
import "../stdlib/libc.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_init.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_register.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_alive_check.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_destruct.caspien"

struct Pair{
	@pub{
		a: mut u8
		b: mut u64
	}
}

struct Box{
	@pub{ v: mut u64 }
}

func check(name: static imut string, ok: mut bool) void{
	unsafe{
		if ok{
			printf("PASS %s\n", name)
		}else{
			printf("FAIL %s\n", name)
		}
	}
	return
}

func mixed(seed: mut u64) mut u64{
	let:<mut u8> a = mut 1
	let b = mut seed
	let:<mut u8> c = mut 2
	let d = mut (seed + 1)
	let:<mut u16> e = mut 3
	let:<mut u32> f = mut 4
	let:<mut u8> g = mut 5
	let h = mut (seed + 2)
	let:<mut u16[3]> arr = mut [10, 20, 30]
	let p = mut Pair{a= 7, b= 900}
	let total = mut 0
	for i in 0..4{
		a = a + 1
		c = c + 2
		e = e + 3
		f = f + 4
		g = g + 5
		b = b + 1
		d = d + 2
		h = h + 3
		total = total + a as u64 + c as u64 + e as u64 + f as u64 + g as u64 + b + d + h
	}
	let x = mut arr[1]
	total = total + x as u64 + p.a as u64 + p.b
	return total
}

@throws
func makeBox(n: mut u64) owns some mut Box{
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	return ?new Box{v= n}
}

@throws
func boxed(n: mut u64) mut u64{
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	let:<mut u8> small = mut 9
	let big = mut (n * 2)
	let:<mut u8> tiny = mut 1
	let:<mut u32> mid = mut wrap:<u32>(n)
	let o = mut ?makeBox(big)
	let result = mut 0
	match Some(o){
		result = o.v + small as u64 + tiny as u64 + mid as u64
	}
	return result
}

// throws through two frames that both have narrow locals declared around the pinned gt_routine_address / gt_error_message slots
@throws
func thrower(x: mut u64) mut u64{
	let:<mut u8> pad1 = mut 1
	let wide = mut x
	let:<mut u8> pad2 = mut 2
	if wide == 0{
		throw "zero!"
	}
	return wide + pad1 as u64 + pad2 as u64
}

@throws
func relay(x: mut u64) mut u64{
	?catch(e){ throw e }
	let:<mut u8> before = mut 3
	let wide = mut ?thrower(x)
	let:<mut u8> after = mut 4
	return wide + before as u64 + after as u64
}

func caught(x: mut u64) mut u64{
	?catch(e){
		let:<mut u8> inCatch = mut 50
		let base = mut 1000
		return base + inCatch as u64
	}
	let:<mut u8> k = mut 7
	let acc = mut 0
	for i in 0..5{
		acc = acc + 1
		acc = acc + acc - acc
	}
	let got = mut ?relay(x)
	return got + k as u64 + acc - 5
}

func callBoxed(n: mut u64) mut u64{
	?catch(e){
		return 0
	}
	let:<mut u8> s1 = mut 5
	let w1 = mut n
	let:<mut u8> s2 = mut 6
	let got = mut ?boxed(w1)
	return got + s1 as u64 + s2 as u64
}

func main() void{
	// expected values computed independently (a Python model of the same u8/u16/u32 arithmetic)
	let r = mut mixed(100)
	check("mixed locals, seed 100", r == 2409)
	let r2 = mut mixed(0)
	check("mixed locals, seed 0", r2 == 1209)
	let bx = mut callBoxed(10)
	check("owns + throw + narrow locals", bx == 20 + 9 + 1 + 10 + 5 + 6)
	let again = mut callBoxed(3)
	check("second call, same frame shape", again == 6 + 9 + 1 + 3 + 5 + 6)
	let okPath = mut caught(10)
	check("no throw through two frames", okPath == 10 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 7)
	let thrown = mut caught(0)
	check("throw through two frames lands in the catch", thrown == 1050)
}
```

### FILE: tests/array_match_test.caspien
```
// A fixed array on the right of `in` / `into` / `for` (bare, no `range(...)`) works like a dyn array does:
// `for match i in arr`, `match i in arr`, `match i into arr` prove the index, and the checked access is allowed.
// The bare form is sugar for `range(arr)` (the array's compile-time length). An out-of-range index skips the block;
// a write under a plain `in` proof is a compile error (not tested here: needs a separate negative fixture).
// Prints one PASS/FAIL line per check and `ALL ARRAY MATCH TESTS PASSED`.
extern printf(static imut string,...) void

let static a = mut [1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5, 5.5]
let static b = mut [1, 2, 3]

func check(name: static imut string, ok: mut bool) void{
	unsafe{
		if ok{
			printf("PASS %s\n", name)
		}else{
			printf("FAIL %s\n", name)
		}
	}
	return
}

func main() void{
	let s = mut 0.0
	let t = mut 0
	let skipped = mut 5
	let sum = mut 0
	unsafe{
		for match i in a{
			s += a[i]
		}
		let k = mut 3
		match k in a{
			s += a[k]
		}
		for match j in b{
			match j into b{
				b[j] = 10
			}
		}
		let q = mut 2
		match q in b{
			t = b[q]
		}
		let far = mut 7
		match far in b{
			skipped = b[far]
		}
		for m in 0..3{
			match m in b{
				sum = sum + b[m]
			}
		}
	}
	let ok1 = mut false
	let ok2 = mut false
	let ok3 = mut false
	let ok4 = mut false
	unsafe{
		ok1 = s == 22.0
		ok2 = t == 10
		ok3 = skipped == 5
		ok4 = sum == 30
	}
	check("for match i in float array", ok1)
	check("match i into array writes", ok2)
	check("out-of-range index skips the block", ok3)
	check("match m in array (plain for over 0..3)", ok4)
	unsafe{
		if ok1{
			if ok2{
				if ok3{
					if ok4{
						printf("ALL ARRAY MATCH TESTS PASSED\n")
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
	return
}
```

### FILE: tests/array_member_shapes_test.caspien
```
// Regression test for (1) an array of structs whose element struct itself has an array member (`h.cells[i].vals[j]`), on the stack and on the heap;
// (2) array members that straddle an 8-byte word boundary of their struct (`u8[5]` at offset 4, `u16[3]` at offset 4, `u8[3]` at offset 6), read through
// an array of structs (the pushed block's words are reversed, so such a member is not contiguous in memory); (3) a local narrow array literal with a
// computed element (`let a: u16[3] = [c, c + 1, c + 7]`), which used to store the pushed words as if they were packed and crash; (4) an array literal that
// mixes a typed variable with plain literals (`[c, 2, c + 7]` with `c: u16` is a `u16[3]`).
// Run with every optimizer switch off and on: identical output.
import "../stdlib/libc.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_init.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_register.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_alive_check.caspien"
import "../stdlib/gt_destruct.caspien"

struct Cell{
	@pub{
		id: mut u8
		vals: mut u16[3]
		z: mut u8
	}
}
struct Holder{
	@pub{
		tag: mut u8
		cells: mut Cell[2]
		tail: mut u16
	}
}
struct Strad{
	@pub{
		a: mut u32
		b: mut u8[5]
		c: mut u32
	}
}
struct StradH{
	@pub{
		tag: mut u8
		ss: mut Strad[2]
		tail: mut u16
	}
}
func check(name: static imut string, ok: mut bool) void{
	unsafe{
		if ok{
			printf("PASS %s\n", name)
		}else{
			printf("FAIL %s\n", name)
		}
	}
	return
}
func stackAos(t: mut u16, c: mut u16, k: mut u8) void{
	let h = mut Holder{tag= 3, cells= [Cell{id= k, vals= [c, c + 1, c + 2], z= 9}, Cell{id= 5, vals= [c - 19, c - 18, c + 7], z= k}], tail= t + 1}
	check("aos stack tag", h.tag == 3)
	check("aos stack c0.id", h.cells[0].id == 4)
	check("aos stack c0.vals[0]", h.cells[0].vals[0] == 20)
	check("aos stack c0.vals[2]", h.cells[0].vals[2] == 22)
	check("aos stack c0.z", h.cells[0].z == 9)
	check("aos stack c1.id", h.cells[1].id == 5)
	check("aos stack c1.vals[1]", h.cells[1].vals[1] == 2)
	check("aos stack c1.vals[2]", h.cells[1].vals[2] == 27)
	check("aos stack c1.z", h.cells[1].z == 4)
	check("aos stack tail", h.tail == 1001)
}
func heapAos(t: mut u16, c: mut u16, k: mut u8) mut u64{
	?catch(e){ return 1 }
	let h = mut ? new Holder{tag= 3, cells= [Cell{id= k, vals= [c, c + 1, c + 2], z= 9}, Cell{id= 5, vals= [c - 19, c - 18, c + 7], z= k}], tail= t + 1}
	match Some(h){
		if h.tag != 3{ return 2 }
		if h.cells[0].id != 4{ return 3 }
		if h.cells[0].vals[1] != 21{ return 4 }
		if h.cells[0].z != 9{ return 5 }
		if h.cells[1].vals[2] != 27{ return 6 }
		if h.cells[1].z != 4{ return 7 }
		if h.tail != 1001{ return 8 }
	}
	return 0
}
func stackStrad(t: mut u16, c: mut u32, k: mut u8) void{
	let s = mut Strad{a= c, b= [k, k + 1, k + 2, k + 3, k + 4], c= c + 1}
	check("strad stack a", s.a == 20)
	check("strad stack b[0]", s.b[0] == 4)
	check("strad stack b[1]", s.b[1] == 5)
	check("strad stack b[3]", s.b[3] == 7)
	check("strad stack b[4]", s.b[4] == 8)
	check("strad stack c", s.c == 21)
	let h = mut StradH{tag= 1, ss= [Strad{a= c, b= [k, k - 2, k - 1, k, k + 1], c= 9}, Strad{a= 7, b= [k + 1, k + 2, k + 3, k + 4, k + 5], c= c + 2}], tail= t + 1}
	check("strad arr tag", h.tag == 1)
	check("strad arr s0.b[0]", h.ss[0].b[0] == 4)
	check("strad arr s0.b[4]", h.ss[0].b[4] == 5)
	check("strad arr s1.a", h.ss[1].a == 7)
	check("strad arr s1.b[0]", h.ss[1].b[0] == 5)
	check("strad arr s1.b[4]", h.ss[1].b[4] == 9)
	check("strad arr s1.c", h.ss[1].c == 22)
	check("strad arr tail", h.tail == 1001)
}
struct Tri{
	@pub{
		a: mut u32
		b: mut u16
		c: mut u8[3]
		d: mut u8
	}
}
struct TriH{
	@pub{
		tag: mut u8
		ts: mut Tri[2]
		tail: mut u16
	}
}
func heapStrad(t: mut u16, c: mut u32, k: mut u8) mut u64{
	?catch(e){ return 1 }
	let h = mut ? new StradH{tag= 1, ss= [Strad{a= c, b= [k, k - 2, k - 1, k, k + 1], c= 9}, Strad{a= 7, b= [k + 1, k + 2, k + 3, k + 4, k + 5], c= c + 2}], tail= t + 1}
	match Some(h){
		if h.tag != 1{ return 2 }
		if h.ss[0].b[0] != 4{ return 3 }
		if h.ss[0].b[4] != 5{ return 4 }
		if h.ss[1].a != 7{ return 5 }
		if h.ss[1].b[0] != 5{ return 6 }
		if h.ss[1].b[4] != 9{ return 7 }
		if h.ss[1].c != 22{ return 8 }
		if h.tail != 1001{ return 9 }
	}
	return 0
}
func stackTri(t: mut u16, c: mut u32, k: mut u8) void{
	let h = mut TriH{tag= 2, ts= [Tri{a= c, b= t, c= [k, k + 1, k + 2], d= k + 3}, Tri{a= c + 1, b= t + 1, c= [k + 4, 5, k + 6], d= 8}], tail= t + 2}
	check("tri arr t0.a", h.ts[0].a == 20)
	check("tri arr t0.b", h.ts[0].b == 1000)
	check("tri arr t0.c[0]", h.ts[0].c[0] == 4)
	check("tri arr t0.c[2]", h.ts[0].c[2] == 6)
	check("tri arr t0.d", h.ts[0].d == 7)
	check("tri arr t1.a", h.ts[1].a == 21)
	check("tri arr t1.c[0]", h.ts[1].c[0] == 8)
	check("tri arr t1.c[1]", h.ts[1].c[1] == 5)
	check("tri arr t1.c[2]", h.ts[1].c[2] == 10)
	check("tri arr t1.d", h.ts[1].d == 8)
	check("tri arr tail", h.tail == 1002)
}
func localArrays(c: mut u16, k: mut u8, w: mut u32) void{
	let:<mut u16[3]> a = mut [c, c + 1, c + 7]
	check("local u16[3] computed: a[0]", a[0] == 20)
	check("local u16[3] computed: a[1]", a[1] == 21)
	check("local u16[3] computed: a[2]", a[2] == 27)
	let:<mut u8[5]> b = mut [k, k + 1, 9, k + 3, 200]
	check("local u8[5] computed: b[0]", b[0] == 4)
	check("local u8[5] computed: b[2]", b[2] == 9)
	check("local u8[5] computed: b[3]", b[3] == 7)
	check("local u8[5] computed: b[4]", b[4] == 200)
	let:<mut u32[2]> d = mut [7, w + 1]
	check("local u32[2] mixed: d[0]", d[0] == 7)
	check("local u32[2] mixed: d[1]", d[1] == 10)
	let:<mut u16[3]> m = mut [c, 2, c + 7]
	check("mixed literal and variable: m[1]", m[1] == 2)
	check("mixed literal and variable: m[2]", m[2] == 27)
}
func main() void{
	let:<mut u16> t = mut 1000
	let:<mut u16> c = mut 20
	let:<mut u32> c32 = mut 20
	let:<mut u32> w = mut 9
	let:<mut u8> k = mut 4
	stackAos(t, c, k)
	check("aos heap", heapAos(t, c, k) == 0)
	stackStrad(t, c32, k)
	check("strad heap", heapStrad(t, c32, k) == 0)
	stackTri(t, c32, k)
	localArrays(c, k, w)
}
```

```
// Regression test: arrays whose ROWS are 3, 5, 6 or 7 bytes (`u8[3]`, `u8[5]`, `u16[3]`, `u8[7]` ...) built from row variables and read back.
// Three separate bugs, all in Codegen: (1) the packed construction stored each odd-sized row with an 8-byte move, so the second row's store
// overwrote the low bytes of the destination address (segfault) and a first row's junk landed in the image; (2) a row that starts in one
// 8-byte word of the pushed block and ends in the next was read with a plain load (the block's words are in reverse order in memory, so the
// bytes above the block were read instead of the second word); (3) a row taken out of an array that fits in one word was cut to one byte.

struct Holder{
	@pub{
		tag: mut u8
		w: mut u16[3][2]
		tail: mut u64
	}
}

func check(name: static imut string, ok: mut bool) void{

			printf("PASS %s\n", name)
		}else{
			printf("FAIL %s\n", name)
		}
	}
	return
}

func main() void{
	// u16[3] rows: 6 bytes, the second row straddles the first and second word
	let:<mut u16[3]> a0 = mut [1, 2, 3]
	let:<mut u16[3]> a1 = mut [4, 5, 6]
	let:<mut u16[3][2]> w = mut [a0, a1]
	let w00 = mut w[0][0]
	let w01 = mut w[0][1]
	let w02 = mut w[0][2]
	let w10 = mut w[1][0]
	let w11 = mut w[1][1]
	let w12 = mut w[1][2]
	check("u16[3][2] row 0", w00 == 1 && w01 == 2 && w02 == 3)
	check("u16[3][2] row 1", w10 == 4 && w11 == 5 && w12 == 6)

	// u8[3] rows: the whole 6-byte array fits in one word
	let:<mut u8[3]> b0 = mut [1, 2, 3]
	let:<mut u8[3]> b1 = mut [4, 5, 6]
	let:<mut u8[3][2]> v = mut [b0, b1]
	let v00 = mut v[0][0]
	let v02 = mut v[0][2]
	let v10 = mut v[1][0]
	let v12 = mut v[1][2]
	check("u8[3][2] row 0", v00 == 1 && v02 == 3)
	check("u8[3][2] row 1", v10 == 4 && v12 == 6)

	// a whole row taken out of the array keeps all its bytes
	let rv = mut v[1]
	let rv0 = mut rv[0]
	let rv1 = mut rv[1]
	let rv2 = mut rv[2]
	check("u8[3] row copied out", rv0 == 4 && rv1 == 5 && rv2 == 6)
	let rw = mut w[1]
	let rw1 = mut rw[1]
	let rw2 = mut rw[2]
	check("u16[3] row copied out", rw1 == 5 && rw2 == 6)

	// u8[5] rows, three of them: 15 bytes, rows start at bytes 0, 5, 10
	let:<mut u8[5]> c0 = mut [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
	let:<mut u8[5]> c1 = mut [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]
	let:<mut u8[5]> c2 = mut [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]
	let:<mut u8[5][3]> c = mut [c0, c1, c2]
	let c04 = mut c[0][4]
	let c10 = mut c[1][0]
	let c14 = mut c[1][4]
	let c20 = mut c[2][0]
	let c24 = mut c[2][4]
	check("u8[5][3] rows", c04 == 5 && c10 == 6 && c14 == 10 && c20 == 11 && c24 == 15)

	// u8[7] rows: 14 bytes, row 1 starts at byte 7
	let:<mut u8[7]> d0 = mut [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
	let:<mut u8[7]> d1 = mut [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]

	let d10 = mut d[1][0]
	let d16 = mut d[1][6]
	check("u8[7][2] rows", d06 == 7 && d10 == 8 && d16 == 14)

	// u16[3] rows, three of them: 18 bytes
	let:<mut u16[3]> e0 = mut [10, 20, 30]
	let:<mut u16[3]> e1 = mut [40, 50, 60]
	let:<mut u16[3]> e2 = mut [70, 80, 90]
	let:<mut u16[3][3]> e = mut [e0, e1, e2]
	let e12 = mut e[1][2]
	let e20 = mut e[2][0]
	let e22 = mut e[2][2]
	check("u16[3][3] rows", e12 == 60 && e20 == 70 && e22 == 90)

	let nw02 = mut w[0][2]
	check("write inside a row", nw10 == 4 && nw11 == 55 && nw12 == 6 && nw02 == 3)
```

```
// Regression test: reading one element of an array whose elements are more than one word but NOT a multiple of 8 bytes (a row of a
// `u32[3][2]` is 12 bytes, an element of a `Tri[]` is 12 bytes) while another value already sits on the stack beneath the read, i.e. the
// value is stored (`let v = mut grid[1][2]`) rather than passed straight to a call. LOOKUP_ARRAY used to shrink the array block by
// (total - elemSize) instead of whole words, leaving rsp 4 bytes off and writing 4 bytes past the old block over the pending store address:
// segfault. Found when function inlining turned `check("..", g[0][0] == 1)` (register argument) into a store.
import "../stdlib/libc.caspien"

struct Grid{
	@pub{
		tag: mut u8
		g: mut u32[3][2]
		tail: mut u64
	}
}

struct Tri{
	@pub{
		a: mut u32
		b: mut u32
		c: mut u32
	}
}

func check(name: static imut string, ok: mut bool) void{
	unsafe{
		if ok{
			printf("PASS %s\n", name)
		}else{
			printf("FAIL %s\n", name)
		}
	}
	return
}

func main() void{
	let:<mut u32[3]> q0 = mut [1, 2, 3]
	let:<mut u32[3]> q1 = mut [4, 5, 6]
	let:<mut u32[3][2]> grid = mut [q0, q1]
	let g1 = mut Grid{tag= 3, g= grid, tail= 1007}

	let v00 = mut grid[0][0]
	let v12 = mut grid[1][2]
	let v10 = mut grid[1][0]
	check("local 2D read stored: [0][0]", v00 == 1)
	check("local 2D read stored: [1][2]", v12 == 6)
	check("local 2D read stored: [1][0]", v10 == 4)

	let s00 = mut g1.g[0][0]
	let s11 = mut g1.g[1][1]
	check("member 2D read stored: [0][0]", s00 == 1)
	check("member 2D read stored: [1][1]", s11 == 5)

	let ok = mut (g1.g[0][0] == 1)
	check("member 2D compare stored", ok)
	let ok2 = mut (grid[1][2] == 6)
	check("local 2D compare stored", ok2)

	// the neighbours of the store target must not be touched
	let before = mut 111
	let mid = mut grid[1][1]
	let after = mut 222
	check("neighbour before", before == 111)
	check("stored value", mid == 5)
	check("neighbour after", after == 222)

	// a 12-byte struct element of an array
	let:<mut Tri[2]> ts = mut [Tri{a= 1, b= 2, c= 3}, Tri{a= 4, b= 5, c= 6}]
	let t1 = mut ts[1]
	let tc = mut t1.c
	check("struct element read stored: c", tc == 6)
	check("struct element read stored: a", t1.a == 4)
	let direct = mut ts[0].b
	check("struct element field stored", direct == 2)

	// every element of the 2D array (rows start mid-word)
	let e10 = mut grid[0][0]
	let e11 = mut grid[0][1]
	let e12 = mut grid[0][2]
	let e20 = mut grid[1][0]
	let e21 = mut grid[1][1]
	let e22 = mut grid[1][2]
	check("all elements in order", e10 == 1 && e11 == 2 && e12 == 3 && e20 == 4 && e21 == 5 && e22 == 6)

	// a read in the middle of a call's argument list, after earlier arguments are already in registers
	unsafe{
		printf("row1: %llu %llu %llu\n", grid[1][0], grid[1][1], grid[1][2])
	}
	check("read as a later argument", grid[1][1] == 5)
	return
}
```

### FILE: tests/bits_ops_check.sh

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Usage: tests/bits_ops_check.sh   (Linux, from anywhere; scratch copy of the tree, target linux)
# Compile-time checks for the bitwise builtins (bits_and / bits_xor / bits_or / bits_not / bits_left / bits_right) and for hex / binary / underscore
# integer literals: wrong arity, non-integer arguments, mismatched widths, literals that do not fit, malformed literals (lex errors), and a few
# forms that must still COMPILE. Each negative case asserts a non-zero exit AND a substring of the message. The runtime behaviour is covered by
# tests/bits_ops_test.caspien.
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"; export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=
T=$(mktemp -d); cp -r "$ROOT"/ASTGenerator "$ROOT"/Optimizer "$ROOT"/LowerOrderGenerator "$ROOT"/Codegen "$ROOT"/stdlib "$ROOT"/Compiler*.class "$ROOT"/Compiler.java "$T"/
sed -e 's/^target windows_gnu/target linux/' -e 's/^    default: win64/    default: sysv_x64/' "$ROOT/toolchain.config" > "$T/toolchain.config"
mkdir -p "$T/tests"; cd "$T"
pass=0; fail=0
# usage: case_ name expect(ok|MESSAGE-SUBSTRING) body-of-main
case_() {
  printf 'func main() void{\n%s\n\treturn\n}\n' "$3" > tests/c_$1.caspien
  out=$(java Compiler -i tests/c_$1.caspien out_$1 2>&1); rc=$?
  if [ "$2" = ok ]; then
    if [ $rc -eq 0 ]; then echo "PASS $1"; pass=$((pass+1)); else echo "FAIL $1 (expected to compile)"; echo "$out" | grep "error" | head -2; fail=$((fail+1)); fi
  else
    if [ $rc -ne 0 ] && echo "$out" | grep -qF -- "$2"; then echo "PASS $1"; pass=$((pass+1)); else echo "FAIL $1 (expected error containing: $2)"; echo "$out" | grep "error" | head -2; fail=$((fail+1)); fi
  fi
}
# ---- builtins: arity
case_ and_one_arg        "'bits_and' takes exactly two arguments, got 1" '	let x = mut bits_and(1)'
case_ xor_three_args     "'bits_xor' takes exactly two arguments, got 3" '	let x = mut bits_xor(1, 2, 3)'
case_ or_zero_args       "'bits_or' takes exactly two arguments, got 0"  '	let x = mut bits_or()'
case_ not_two_args       "'bits_not' takes exactly one argument, got 2"  '	let x = mut bits_not(1, 2)'
case_ not_zero_args      "'bits_not' takes exactly one argument, got 0"  '	let x = mut bits_not()'
case_ left_one_arg       "'bits_left' takes exactly two arguments, got 1" '	let x = mut bits_left(1)'
# ---- builtins: operand types
case_ and_float          "'bits_and' requires an integer type, got 'mut_f32'" '	let f = mut 1.5
	let x = mut bits_and(f, f)'
case_ not_float          "'bits_not' requires an integer type, got 'mut_f32'" '	let f = mut 1.5
	let x = mut bits_not(f)'
case_ not_bool           "'bits_not' requires an integer type, got 'mut_bool'" '	let b = mut true
	let x = mut bits_not(b)'
case_ not_string         "'bits_not' requires an integer type" '	let x = mut bits_not("a")'
case_ shift_float        "'bits_left' requires an integer type, got 'mut_f32'" '	let f = mut 1.5
	let x = mut bits_left(f, 1)'
case_ xor_mismatched     "'bits_xor' requires both sides to be the same integer type, got 'mut_u64' and 'mut_u8'" '	let a = mut 1
	let:<mut u8> c = mut 3
	let x = mut bits_xor(a, c)'
case_ and_mismatched_s   "requires both sides to be the same integer type" '	let:<mut s8> a = mut 1
	let:<mut s16> c = mut 3
	let x = mut bits_and(a, c)'
case_ and_signedness     "requires both sides to be the same integer type" '	let:<mut s32> a = mut 1
	let:<mut u32> c = mut 3

# ---- builtins: literal operands must fit the other operand's type
case_ lit_right_too_big  "'bits_xor': literal 300 does not fit in 'u8'" '	let:<mut u8> c = mut 3

case_ dec_over_u64       "does not fit in any integer type (the largest, u64, ends at 18446744073709551615)" '	let x = mut 18446744073709551616'
case_ hex_literal_into_u8 "doesn't satisfy the declared bound 'mut_u8'" '	let:<mut u8> x = mut 0x1FF'
case_ bin_literal_into_u8 "doesn't satisfy the declared bound 'mut_u8'" '	let:<mut u8> x = mut 0b100000000'
# ---- forms that must compile
case_ ok_all_builtins    ok '	let:<mut u8> a = mut 0xF0
	let:<mut u8> b = mut bits_and(a, 0x3C)
	let:<mut u8> c = mut bits_xor(b, 0b1010)
	let:<mut u8> d = mut bits_or(c, 1)
	let:<mut u8> e = mut bits_not(d)
	let:<mut u8> f = mut bits_left(e, 3)
	let:<mut u8> g = mut bits_right(f, 1)'
case_ ok_signed          ok '	let:<mut s16> a = mut -0x7FFF
	let:<mut s16> b = mut bits_not(a)
	let:<mut s16> c = mut bits_right(b, 2)'
case_ ok_literal_both_sides ok '	let:<mut u16> a = mut 7
	let:<mut u16> b = mut bits_and(0xFFFF, a)'
case_ ok_u64_max_hex     ok '	let x = mut 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
	let y = mut bits_not(x)'
case_ ok_underscores     ok '	let x = mut 1_000_000
	let y = mut 0xFF_FF
	let z = mut 0b1111_0000'
echo "bits_ops_check: $pass passed, $fail failed"
rm -rf "$T"
[ $fail -eq 0 ]
```
